kvarner.note: Nine households of the name on the Kvarner, from 1626 to 1855, in two towns twelve kilometres apart. **None of them is joined to another by a record.** They are **not, however, farmers**: the Hungarian state records name a harbour master of Fiume, a draughtsman who drew the imperial salt office at Bakar in 1827, and two naval officers of the name. They are set out in the order the register produced them, with the broken rungs marked for what they are — the places where a join looks likely and is not written down. Read the mothers' surnames with care: on four of these the indexer has copied the father's name into the mother's field, which is why so many of these men appear to have married a woman of their own name.

cards.says: The oldest household the archive holds anywhere. Six children at Rijeka under a Venetian-Latin hand — *Gioannis Antonÿ*, with the trema the scribe put there. This one has been read on the page.

**Ten children, and five of them buried in the year they were born.** Mattio and Nicolò both dead in 1742, Antonio dead 1 September 1753, Aloysia dead 14 September 1757, Maria dead in the same year. The five without dates are the baptisms; the five with them are the burials. This is what a mid-century Kvarner household actually looked like in the register.

rung.text: **A hundred and ten years with nothing in them.** Between Lutia's last child in 1632 and Valentino's first in 1742 the index holds no Defranceschi at Rijeka at all. Whether these are one family across four unrecorded generations or two arrivals a century apart, nothing here can say.

cards.says: Four children, and the index has entered the eldest twice — once from his baptism on 22 November 1772 and once from his burial on 22 August 1775. **Valentino, named for the man fathering at Rijeka thirty years earlier, died at two years and nine months.** The second Ellena, born 1775, was dead by 2 March 1776; the first, born 11 July 1774, is not in the burial book.

rung.text: Giuseppe naming his first son **Valentino** in 1772, when a Valentino was fathering in the same town in 1742–57, is the ordinary grandfather-to-grandson pattern. It is the best reason to think these two households are one family — and it is a naming habit, not a record.

kids.name: Franciscum Josephum Aloysium Joannem Nepomuc Defranceschi
Antonium Petrum Nataliem Joannem Kepomuc Defranceschi

cards.says: **Twelve children in eleven years**, and nine of them carry *Nepomucena* or *Nepomuc* — John of Nepomuk, the Bohemian saint the Habsburgs pushed hard through their new lands. A family naming every child for the dynasty's saint, in the Hungarian crown's free port, is not a peasant household. Three died small: Giosefa in 1797, Anna in 1800, Maria in 1804.

rung.text: The obvious chain would run Valentino → Giuseppe → Valentino. **It does not close.** The one boy who could carry it, Giuseppe's Valentino, was buried in 1775, nineteen years before this household begins. If this Valentino is Giuseppe's son he is a later one, born after 1775, and no record of him has been found.

cards.says: Two entries, one child — Pietro Paolo, baptised and buried in the same year. The surname has lost its prefix: *Franceschi*, not *Defranceschi*, in both hands.
The name moves twelve kilometres down the coast to Bakar, written in the registers by its Latin name *Vitipolis*. Ludovicus, born 1836, lived to 1 June 1855 and died at nineteen.

rung.text: Rijeka and Bakar are one bay apart and shared a diocese, and the name appears at Bakar only after it thins at Rijeka. **Nothing joins them.** The Bakar books have not been read.

cards.says: **Twins, and a week that took two children.** Anna Francisca Catharina and Franciscus Andreas were both baptised on 10 November 1849. Carolo was buried on the 14th and Anna on the 17th. The father is entered as *Francisci Defranceschi **Regii*** — of the king — which in the Hungarian free port means an office, not a farm — and the Hungarian state's own pension rolls name a **Defranceschi Ferencz, harbour master of Fiume**, retired 1857 after forty-two years; and he is married to a second Bellinich, Carolina, where the 1836 household names Catharina.

rung.text: *Franciscus × Catharina Bellinich* in 1836 and *Francisci Regii × Carolinæ Bellinich* in 1849 are almost certainly **one man and two sisters** — the widower marrying his wife's sister. **And the office is no longer a guess.** The Hungarian parliamentary pension schedule of 1872 names **Defranceschi Ferencz, révkapitány — harbour master — of the Fiume Maritime Authority**, with 42 years and 10 months of service and a pension from 1857. *Ferencz* is Franciscus. Forty-three years back from 1857 puts him in state service by about 1814, which makes him the right age to be fathering at Bakar in 1836 and 1849.

cards.says: Two daughters, Maria Dorothea and Antonia, with no year on either. The last of the name at Bakar in the index.

kvarner.missing:
Two books and a third thing. **The Rijeka marriage register** would give each of these men a father and a bride's family, and would close or break the Valentino chain in an afternoon. **The Bakar baptisms** would say whether Franciscus of 1836 and Francisci Regii of 1849 are one man. Neither has been read by this archive; both survive.

**And now a third, which is open and free and merely unworked.** Hungaricana holds **196 entries for Julius Defranceschi** in the k. u. k. navy rank lists between 1894 and 1909 — a complete officer's career, ship by ship and rank by rank, that nobody has yet sat down and transcribed. It also holds Ferencz's pension schedule, Francziska's twelve years of state charity, and Anton's 1827 plan of the Bakar salt office. That is a week's honest work on material that costs nothing.

officials.heading: And what the Hungarian state records say they did
officials.note:
Fiume and Bakar were **Hungarian crown land**, not Austrian and not Croatian, so the men who held office there are in Hungarian paperwork. This archive never looked until 13 September 2026. Everything below is documented, and none of it was here yesterday.

**One caution, and it opens a door.** The 1888 account names Gentile Marussig as the orphan of a *«volt **fiumei** révkapitány»* — a former harbour master **of Fiume** — and in the very next line names Francziska Defranceschi as the orphan of a *révkapitány* with **no port given**. So Ferencz's post is placed by his authority and not by his town. The Fiume Maritime Authority governed the whole Hungarian Littoral, **Bakar included** — which means his port may have been Bakar itself, where the name is fathering in 1836 and 1849.

rows.what: Drew the **«Bauriss der zu Buccari befündlichen aerarial Salz-Einnehmer und Controlors Wohnung»** — the ground plan and section of the imperial salt-receiver's and comptroller's residence at Bakar. Manuscript, 56 × 45 cm, one sheet.
rows.where: National Archives of Hungary, T 62 No 1642, out of E 96 Tricesimalia 1827, 4:51

rows.what: **Révkapitány — port captain — in the service of the Fiume Maritime Authority.** The parliamentary pension schedule of 1872 gives him 42 years, 10 months and 5 days of public service and a pension of 1,050 forints from 1857, which puts him into state service about 1814. The later accounts style him ***m. kir.* révkapitány** — *magyar királyi*, Royal Hungarian — which is the exact Hungarian counterpart of the *Regii* written beside the name at Bakar in 1849.
rows.where: Képviselőházi irományok, 1872, XV. kötet, 1872-650, p. 106; Állami zárszámadás 1894, p. 387

rows.what: «*Defranceschi Ferencz révkapitány árva leánya*» — the port captain's orphan daughter, on a **kegydíj of 65 forints** a year, granted for three-year terms and renewed again and again. The 1898 account gives the reason in the state's own words: **«tekintettel vagyontalanságára, munka- és keresetképtelenségére»** — in view of her destitution, and her incapacity for work or earning. Her 1891 grant expired on **16 October 1894** and was renewed; she was still on the list in 1900.
rows.where: Állami zárszámadás 1888, p. 179; 1894, p. 387; 1898, p. 412; 1900, p. 399; Képviselőházi irományok 1892

rows.what: **K. K. Kriegs-Marine, Marine-Direktion at Pola.** And *Valentin* is the one forename that runs through the Rijeka households — a Valentino fathering there in 1742–57, and another in 1794–1805.

**k. u. k. Kriegsmarine.** He appears **196 times** across fifteen years of rank and distribution lists, by 1909 a *Linienschiffsleutnant*. A complete naval career, open and free, and not yet transcribed.
rows.where: Rangs- und Eintheilungs-Listen der k. u. k. Kriegs-Marine, 1894–1909
Schematismus der K. K. Landwehr und der K. K. Gendarmerie, Wien 1909

officials.close: **Which re-reads the saints.** This archive noted this morning that nine of the twelve children born to Valentino and Ursula at Rijeka between 1794 and 1805 carry *Nepomucena* or *Nepomuc*, and read it as Habsburg dynastic piety. That is half of it. **John of Nepomuk is the saint invoked against drowning** — the patron of bridges, and of men whose work is on the water. In a harbour master's town, a family that names nine children for him is not only being loyal. It is being careful.

southistria.note: Nine households of the name in one southern-Istrian parish across two hundred and twenty-four years, and **not one of them is joined to another by a record**. This is the archive's richest material and its emptiest tree. What follows is everything there is, in order, with every gap measured — because a web drawn honestly is worth more than a pedigree drawn hopefully. The place reads «Croazia, Austria» in the index on all of these; the parish is Svetvinčenat, resolved from the film, not from the place field.

cards.says: The household the archive has leant on hardest. Four children, and the godparents standing for them are Nadal, Batta, Andrea and Nardo De Franceschi — men of the same name in the same parish in the same decade.

rung.text: **Thirty-nine years above this household there is a baptism.** Elena di Franceschi, 21 December 1628, read on the page at Svetvinčenat — the earliest of the name anywhere in Istria that this archive has seen with its own eyes. She is not joined to anyone below her.

cards.says: Gasparo's three children begin eighteen years after Anto's last. A brother, a son, a cousin or a stranger — the register does not say.

rung.text: Anto's last child is 1674; Gasparo's first is 1692. **Nothing links them.** The one book that would — the Svetvinčenat marriage register — runs 1581–89 and 1622–23 and then jumps to 1762. The century that matters is not in it.

cards.says: Piero's household overlaps Gasparo's by fourteen years. Two men of the name fathering in one parish at one time is the ordinary shape of brothers, or of cousins.

rung.text: Overlapping households are **evidence of a family, not of a descent**. Two men fathering side by side cannot be put in sequence.

cards.says: Mattio, two children, sixteen years after Piero's last.
Nadal — the same forename as one of the godparents standing at Anto's baptisms sixty years earlier. A grandson's name, or a common name in a small parish.

rung.text: **Nadal is the only forename that recurs across the whole web.** It stands as a godparent in the 1660s and as a father in the 1730s. That is either the naming thread that ties the parish together, or it is two men who happened to share a saint's day. It is the single thing most worth testing.

cards.says: A century later, and the register has become tabular and Austrian. Six children to Antonio and Maria Bergamo — and the Bergamo family marries into this one twice.

rung.text: **Ninety years of silence** between Nadal's last child in 1735 and Antonio's first in 1825. This is where the web breaks in two.

cards.says: Francesca Defranceschi married Giovanni Bergamo and had seven children. This archive once printed her as the wife of Antonius Cerneca; that was wrong, and the error came from the tabular register's four parent columns being flattened into one list by the index. The correction stands.
Giacoma De Franceschi married Gio Battista Crosilla. Two children. A second Defranceschi daughter marrying out in the same six years as Francesca.
Joannes and Dominica Clagnan, four children, at the very end of the Austrian century. The last household of the name in this group.

rung.text: No join shown to anything above.

southistria.missing: **One book, and it is the one that is missing.** The Svetvinčenat marriage register covers 1581–1589 and 1622–1623, and then nothing until 1762. Every join on this page falls inside that hole. If a second copy of the seventeenth-century marriages survives — in the bishop's archive at Poreč, or among the Venetian provveditore's papers — this web becomes a tree in a week. If it does not, these nine households stay nine households, and the archive should go on saying so.

dalmatia.note: Eight households at Omiš between 1639 and 1887 — and one of them is another one, counted twice. They are set out in the order the index produced them. This is the parish evidence that sits underneath the family's own seventeen-generation chart, gathered independently of it; where the two touch is marked.

cards.says: The oldest Dalmatian household. Margarita baptised 4 March 1639. The index gives this couple a span of 1639 to 1867, which is not a marriage but a collision — a later record of the same two common names swept in with the earlier ones.
Franco and Lucretia, three children, one of them a **Zuanne born 24 May 1646** — the same forename as the head of the household above, in the same town in the same decade.

rung.text: Zuanne fathering from 1639 and a Zuanne born to Franco in 1646 are the naming pattern of **brothers, or of an uncle and his nephew**. It is the only thread between the two seventeenth-century Omiš households, and it is a forename.

cards.says: Gerolimo and Elena, two daughters, no year on either. Gerolimo is the name the nineteenth-century households give their first sons.

rung.text: **Two hundred and eight years with nothing in them.** Between Franco's children in 1646 and Francesco's first in 1854, this archive holds no Omiš household at all. The town's registers exist; they have not been read.

cards.says: **Seventeen children in twenty-three years** — the largest household in this archive. Giovanni Giuseppe Maria first, on 29 December 1854; the names run four and five deep, Rados Niccoló Maria, Giovanni Girolamo Andrea Felice.

**This is the household above, counted twice.** Six of these seven children are the same named individuals as in Francesco and Maria's list; the place differs only in language, Almissa being the Italian for Omiš; and the mother's surname differs by one letter, *De Caralipeo* against *De Caralipco*. **The seventh, Carlo Paolo Michele Maria, appears only here** — so the true household is not seventeen children but eighteen.

rung.text: **A duplicate, now identified.** The households list has carried this family twice since it was built, because the FamilySearch index writes the same town in two languages and two indexers read one surname differently. Flagged in the data; the merge is a separate job because the household ids are referenced elsewhere.

cards.says: Giovanni and Maria Ipsich, seven children, overlapping Francesco's household by fourteen years. Their first, Girolamo, was born and buried in 1860.

rung.text: **Three households fathering at Omiš at once** — Francesco from 1854, Giovanni from 1860, Niccoló and a second Giovanni from 1873 — and the first sons are called Girolamo and Niccoló, which are the names in the undated Gerolimo household. Brothers is the obvious reading. The Omiš marriage register would prove it.

cards.says: Niccoló and Teresa, five children, beginning with Riccardo Feligiano Maria on 9 June 1873.

A second Giovanni, with Giovanna Baucich — and **Baučić is the surname the family's own chart gives to Ivan's wife in the generation of 1829–1895.** The made chart and the parish index touch here, and this is the clearest place they do.

rung.text: Where «Rodoslovno stablo obitelji Franceschi» says *Ivan, 1829–1895, wife Ivanica Baučić*, the index says *Giovanni Franceschi × Giovanna Baucich, three children at Omiš 1873–1879*. Ivanica and Giovanna are the same name in two languages. **This is the join between the family's chart and the public record** — and it is an agreement, not a proof.

dalmatia.missing: **The Omiš marriage register.** Three men of the name fathering in the town at the same time in the 1860s and 70s, with first sons called Girolamo and Niccoló, is the shape of brothers — and one line in a marriage book would say whose sons they were. It would also test the chart's Ivan × Ivanica Baučić against the index's Giovanni × Giovanna Baucich, which is the single most useful thing anyone could do for this family. **And the two hundred and eight years between 1646 and 1854 are simply unread**, not lost.
